tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST — CURVED AXIS, LONG SPREADING BRANCHES
tiles.details: The real Matt Lavin images show long narrow branches arising along one curved axis, not independent stems. Regional sources report roughly 3–13 branches in Texas and 5–10 in a Montana guide; the count varies. Photograph the rooted crown and complete head with a centimeter scale. The mature head may detach and tumble, so a loose head is not proof of its rooted parent.
tiles.short: Low perennial tuft; stiff curved central flowering axis carries several long, widely divergent, slender lateral racemes.
tiles.status: REAL SOURCE FLOWERING ARCHITECTURE — NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO SAME ROOTED PLANT

tiles.heading: 02 · LIGULE, COLLAR AND GROWTH FORM
tiles.details: At the same flowering plant open the blade–sheath junction; photograph the free papery ligule with a 1-mm ruler and distinguish it from blade-edge hairs. Texas Silveus describes an approximately 3-mm membrane, while Montana gives ~1–1.5 mm. Leaves are narrow and may spiral as they dry. No existing gallery image proves the ligule, roots, or measured leaf margin.
tiles.short: Perennial bunchgrass without obvious rhizomes; true ligule an eciliate membrane, about 1–4 mm in regional descriptions.
tiles.status: PUBLISHED VEGETATIVE TRAITS — NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO TRUE LIGULE/CROWN

tiles.heading: 03 · ONE-FLOWERED SPIKELETS — INSPECT THE BRANCH FACE
tiles.details: Use a 10–20× view of a mature attached raceme and a 1-mm scale; identify each spikelet insertion, its attachment side and one floret. Kew/GrassBase and the historic Texas treatment describe a unilateral/one-sided arrangement, but an Arizona Extension page also describes alternating spikelets on opposite sides. This wording conflict requires a specimen-backed image before a precise row-orientation arrow or categorical crew shortcut. The current branch photos do not resolve the rows.
tiles.short: One-flowered, sessile spikelets usually about 3–4 mm in modern Montana/Kew descriptions; older Texas treatment allows ~3–6 mm.
tiles.status: SOURCE WORDING CONFLICT — NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO RACHIS INSERTIONS BOTH FACES

tiles.heading: 04 · SEPARATE GLUMES, THREE-VEINED LEMMA AND AWNLET
tiles.details: Older Texas Silveus reports short glume awn tips variably present; Kew GrassBase emphasizes narrow acuminate glumes and an acute three-veined lemma. Montana describes lemma ~2–4 mm, awnless or awn-tipped. Distinguish a glume point or awnlet from a true long lemma awn. Measure several mature one-flowered spikelets, detach and photograph each glume and dorsal lemma with a 1-mm ruler; no organ-level arrows are justified from the present wide photographs.
tiles.short: Two narrow 1-veined glumes; Texas treatment gives lower ~2–4 mm, upper ~2.5–6 mm; three-veined fertile lemma ~3–5 mm.
tiles.status: PUBLISHED MEASUREMENTS — NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO MEASURED SPIKELET DISSECTION

tiles.heading: 05 · CENTRAL TEXAS LOOK-ALIKES — DO NOT IDENTIFY BY A WIRE HEAD ALONE
tiles.details: Lindheimer muhly has a denser upright flowering panicle; nimblewill has a small narrow contracted panicle; purple lovegrass produces a diffuse airy cloud. Tumblegrass requires its distinctive whole branching pattern plus mature spikelet attachments, true ligule and one-flowered anatomy. Do not infer a species from an old detached tumbling seedhead or a close-up of one branch alone.
tiles.short: Sideoats grama has many short pendent side branches; tumblegrass has fewer long, rigid, widely diverging racemes on a curved axis.
tiles.status: SOURCE-BASED LOOK-ALIKE LESSON — MATCHED COMPARISON PHOTOS PENDING

tiles.heading: 06 · PUBLIC-READY GATE — PHOTO AND SITE HANDOFFS
tiles.details: NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO (Grass Photo-Finish): a vouchered rooted Central Texas tuft plus complete curved head; two opposite faces of ONE attached raceme with 1-mm scale to document actual spikelet orientation; true ~1–4 mm membranous ligule on same specimen; mature dissected 3–6 mm spikelet with both glumes and three-veined lemma, awn tips resolved. NEEDS_SITE_QA (Public Learner Readiness): verify all three archived JPEGs, per-photo CC BY-NC/CC BY-SA 2.0 rights, EXIF/GPS removal, original two gross arrows, correct scientific synonym, six tile rendering, and rights-filtered public gallery. No new images, arrows, genus/family edits or Pages actions. Do not claim 100% until scientific orientation discrepancy and anatomical pixels are resolved.
tiles.short: FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS: three existing archived source photographs, three species teaching panels; fine anatomy remains unverified.

steps.title: 1 · First, recognize the plant
steps.look_for: TUMBLEGRASS (long treated as Schedonnardus paniculatus) has a DISTINCTIVE architecture: a low tuft with long, often stiff curved flowering axis and several long, very slender, widely diverging one-sided racemes. On a mature raceme, spikelets sit in TWO ROWS along one side of the axis. Look at the whole branch pattern FIRST; then confirm that unilateral spikelet arrangement and membranous ligule. Old dry heads may detach and tumble.
steps.why_it_matters: Start with the recorded recognition characters before making a species identification.

steps.title: 2 · Examine the whole plant
steps.look_for: START with the physically archived Matt Lavin photograph: trace the long slender divergent branches arising from a curved central flowering axis, rather than mistaking each branch for an independent flowering stem.
steps.why_it_matters: Habit and growing context are supporting evidence, not proof of hidden roots or rhizomes.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect leaves, collar and nodes
steps.look_for: At the same flowering plant open the blade–sheath junction; photograph the free papery ligule with a 1-mm ruler and distinguish it from blade-edge hairs. Texas Silveus describes an approximately 3-mm membrane, while Montana gives ~1–1.5 mm. Leaves are narrow and may spiral as they dry. No existing gallery image proves the ligule, roots, or measured leaf margin.
steps.why_it_matters: Examine the real structures; the photo may not expose or measure all the described characters.

steps.title: 4 · Check the flowering structure
steps.look_for: Use a 10–20× view of a mature attached raceme and a 1-mm scale; identify each spikelet insertion, its attachment side and one floret. Kew/GrassBase and the historic Texas treatment describe a unilateral/one-sided arrangement, but an Arizona Extension page also describes alternating spikelets on opposite sides. This wording conflict requires a specimen-backed image before a precise row-orientation arrow or categorical crew shortcut. The current branch photos do not resolve the rows.
steps.why_it_matters: Use an attached, correctly identified specimen when deciding the flower or spikelet structures.

steps.title: 5 · Compare similar grasses
steps.look_for: Tumblegrass long divergent one-sided racemes are not the densely packed panicle of Lindheimer, nor the short narrow contracted panicle of nimblewill. Sideoats grama bears MANY short pendent lateral spikes along a flowering axis rather than a few long thin stiff racemes. Purple lovegrass has a diffuse branching cloud with spikelets dispersed on very fine branches, not distinctive straight unilateral racemes.
steps.why_it_matters: Confirm at least two independent botanical characters; do not remove a native candidate from color alone.

panels.label: TUMBLEGRASS — archived branching inflorescence detail
panels.caption: Follow the narrow flowering branch to its attachment on the curved reddish flowering axis. Both arrows identify visible gross structures in the archived image, not a glume, lemma or individual spikelet. Matt Lavin photographed this Montana plant as Schedonnardus paniculatus (the source name retained in the photo record); exact source identification is not independently vouchered for Hays County. The image does not show the true ligule or microscopic unilateral spikelet rows.

intro: TUMBLEGRASS (long treated as Schedonnardus paniculatus) has a DISTINCTIVE architecture: a low tuft with long, often stiff curved flowering axis and several long, very slender, widely diverging one-sided racemes. On a mature raceme, spikelets sit in TWO ROWS along one side of the axis. Look at the whole branch pattern FIRST; then confirm that unilateral spikelet arrangement and membranous ligule. Old dry heads may detach and tumble.
memory_rule: A few LONG stiff, widely spreading racemes — not a fluffy cloud or short sideoats spikes.
safety_note: 2026-10-27 new pixel-inspected source JPEGS document a close unilateral spikelet branch and true outer sheath junction. No sub-mm free ligule, actual fibrous root origin, calibrated separated glumes/lemmas or specimen voucher has been established. Individual NC images are conditioned on actual noncommercial reuse.
field_rule: Curved flowering axis + long widely spreading one-sided slender branches + appressed unilateral spikelets; confirm an eciliate membrane ligule and single-flowered spikelet at scale.
photo_data_caution: Missing or restricted comparison photographs have not been replaced by guesses. Source statements are not proof the associated structure is visible in any available photo.
comparison_text: Tumblegrass long divergent one-sided racemes are not the densely packed panicle of Lindheimer, nor the short narrow contracted panicle of nimblewill. Sideoats grama bears MANY short pendent lateral spikes along a flowering axis rather than a few long thin stiff racemes. Purple lovegrass has a diffuse branching cloud with spikelets dispersed on very fine branches, not distinctive straight unilateral racemes.
